claim: The study included more than 100,000 patients from 28 countries.
source: Our analysis, that includes more than 100,000 patients from 28 countries, suggests that in many settings patients hospitalised with Omicron variant infection less often presented with commonly reported symptoms compared to patients infected with pre-Omicron variants.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of patients and countries included in the analysis.

claim: Patients hospitalised with Omicron variant infection less often presented with commonly reported symptoms compared to patients infected with pre-Omicron variants in many settings.
source: Our analysis, that includes more than 100,000 patients from 28 countries, suggests that in many settings patients hospitalised with Omicron variant infection less often presented with commonly reported symptoms compared to patients infected with pre-Omicron variants.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of the study data.

claim: Patients with COVID-19 admitted to hospital after Omicron variant emergence had lower mortality compared to patients admitted during the period when Omicron variant was responsible for only a minority of infections (odds ratio 0.67 [95% confidence interval 0.61–0.75]).
source: Patients with COVID-19 admitted to hospital after Omicron variant emergence had lower mortality compared to patients admitted during the period when Omicron variant was responsible for only a minority of infections (odds ratio in a mixed-effects logistic regression adjusted for likely confounders, 0.67 [95% confidence interval 0.61–0.75]).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mixed-effects logistic regression analysis.

claim: The emergence of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants represents a threat to the long-term control of COVID-19.
source: The emergence of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants represents a threat to the long-term control of COVID-19 (Fontanet et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fontanet et al., 2021.

claim: Efforts to develop vaccines that protect against severe disease have been successful.
source: Whilst efforts to develop vaccines that protect against severe disease have been successful (Polack et al., 2020; Voysey et al., 2021; Baden et al., 2021), mutations in the viral genome that lead to ability to escape immunity, and increased transmissibility and/or clinical severity, either via intrinsic virulence or reduced vaccine effectiveness (Lopez Bernal et al., 2021), have the potential to cause substantial disease burden despite high vaccine coverage in many countries (Our World in Data, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Polack et al., 2020; Voysey et al., 2021; Baden et al., 2021.

claim: Mutations in the viral genome that lead to ability to escape immunity, and increased transmissibility and/or clinical severity have the potential to cause substantial disease burden despite high vaccine coverage.
source: Whilst efforts to develop vaccines that protect against severe disease have been successful (Polack et al., 2020; Voysey et al., 2021; Baden et al., 2021), mutations in the viral genome that lead to ability to escape immunity, and increased transmissibility and/or clinical severity, either via intrinsic virulence or reduced vaccine effectiveness (Lopez Bernal et al., 2021), have the potential to cause substantial disease burden despite high vaccine coverage in many countries (Our World in Data, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lopez Bernal et al., 2021 and Our World in Data, 2021.

claim: Early data from South Africa showed reduced severity of Omicron lineage BA.1.
source: Early data from South Africa showed reduced severity of Omicron lineage BA.1 and similar results were reported in the United Kingdom and the United States (Wolter et al., 2022; Lewnard et al., 2022; Nyberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wolter et al., 2022; Lewnard et al., 2022; Nyberg et al., 2022.

claim: Similar results of reduced severity were reported in the United Kingdom and the United States.
source: Early data from South Africa showed reduced severity of Omicron lineage BA.1 and similar results were reported in the United Kingdom and the United States (Wolter et al., 2022; Lewnard et al., 2022; Nyberg et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wolter et al., 2022; Lewnard et al., 2022; Nyberg et al., 2022.

claim: The impact of new variants in terms of clinical consequences is context-specific due to regional differences in disease epidemiology.
source: However, the impact, in terms of clinical consequences (i.e. disease severity), of new variants has been shown to be context-specific, due to regional differences in disease epidemiology, including local circulation of previous variants and their cumulative incidences, variable vaccination coverages, and heterogeneity in population-level frequencies of risk factors (e.g. frequency of comorbidities) for severe disease and mortality.
evidence: This is a statement about the context-specific nature of variant impacts based on epidemiological understanding.

claim: International studies with standardised protocols are necessary to allow comparative assessments across different countries and epidemiological contexts.
source: For this reason, international studies with standardised protocols are necessary to allow comparative assessments across different countries and epidemiological contexts.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the context-specific nature of variant impacts.

claim: Overall, 129,196 records from patients admitted to hospital between 1st October 2021 and 28th February 2022 were included in this analysis.
source: Overall, 129,196 records from patients admitted to hospital between 1st October 2021 and 28th February 2022 were included in this analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study population.

claim: Clinical centres in 30 countries contributed data.
source: Clinical centres in 30 countries contributed data (median 53 observations per country, interquartile range [IQR] 18–162); 11 countries contributed data on more than 100 hospitalised clinical cases (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of countries contributing data.

claim: The median number of observations per country was 53 with an interquartile range of 18–162.
source: Clinical centres in 30 countries contributed data (median 53 observations per country, interquartile range [IQR] 18–162); 11 countries contributed data on more than 100 hospitalised clinical cases (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the distribution of observations per country.

claim: 11 countries contributed data on more than 100 hospitalised clinical cases.
source: Clinical centres in 30 countries contributed data (median 53 observations per country, interquartile range [IQR] 18–162); 11 countries contributed data on more than 100 hospitalised clinical cases (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of countries with substantial data contributions.

claim: 54.0% of records were from South Africa.
source: A total of 54.0% and 42.6% of records were from South Africa and the United Kingdom, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of records from South Africa.

claim: 42.6% of records were from the United Kingdom.
source: A total of 54.0% and 42.6% of records were from South Africa and the United Kingdom, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of records from the United Kingdom.

claim: 103,061 patients from 28/30 countries were admitted either in the two months before the Omicron variant represented 10% of infections or in the two months after the Omicron variant was responsible for at least 90% of the infections.
source: Using information presented in Figure 1, 103,061 patients, from 28/30 countries, were admitted either in the two months before the Omicron variant represented 10% of infections at the country-level (N=22,921; henceforth, the pre-Omicron period) or in the two months after (N=80,140) the Omicron variant was responsible for at least 90% of the infections; for ease of reference, the latter period will be referred to as the Omicron period.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study population in the defined periods.

claim: 22,921 patients were admitted in the pre-Omicron period.
source: Using information presented in Figure 1, 103,061 patients, from 28/30 countries, were admitted either in the two months before the Omicron variant represented 10% of infections at the country-level (N=22,921; henceforth, the pre-Omicron period) or in the two months after (N=80,140) the Omicron variant was responsible for at least 90% of the infections; for ease of reference, the latter period will be referred to as the Omicron period.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of patients in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: 80,140 patients were admitted in the Omicron period.
source: Using information presented in Figure 1, 103,061 patients, from 28/30 countries, were admitted either in the two months before the Omicron variant represented 10% of infections at the country-level (N=22,921; henceforth, the pre-Omicron period) or in the two months after (N=80,140) the Omicron variant was responsible for at least 90% of the infections; for ease of reference, the latter period will be referred to as the Omicron period.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of patients in the Omicron period.

claim: 12,085 patients were admitted during weeks between the end of the pre-Omicron period and the start of the Omicron period and are not included in analyses.
source: Note that 12,085 patients were admitted during weeks between the end of the pre-Omicron period and the start of the Omicron period and are not included in analyses presented in the following subsections (Figure 2); and 12,560 records of patients admitted two months after Omicron variant represented 90% of infections were not analysed.
evidence: This is a direct statement about patients excluded from the analysis.

claim: 12,560 records of patients admitted two months after Omicron variant represented 90% of infections were not analysed.
source: Note that 12,085 patients were admitted during weeks between the end of the pre-Omicron period and the start of the Omicron period and are not included in analyses presented in the following subsections (Figure 2); and 12,560 records of patients admitted two months after Omicron variant represented 90% of infections were not analysed.
evidence: This is a direct statement about patients excluded from the analysis.

claim: All patients from South Africa, the United Kingdom and Malaysia were assumed to be SARS-CoV-2 positive, as this is one criterion for inclusion in their databases.
source: All patients from South Africa, the United Kingdom and Malaysia were assumed to be SARS-CoV-2 positive, as this is one criterion for inclusion in their databases.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the inclusion criteria for certain countries.

claim: The median age of patients during the pre-Omicron period was 62 years (IQR 43 – 76).
source: The median (IQR) ages of patients during the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods were 62 (43 – 76) and 50 (30 – 72) years, respectively; however, country-specific medians suggest that the younger age of patients after Omicron variant emergence in the combined dataset is at least partially explained by an increase in the proportion of data contributed by South Africa, relative to the proportion of data contributed by other countries (Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the median age in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: The median age of patients during the Omicron period was 50 years (IQR 30 – 72).
source: The median (IQR) ages of patients during the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods were 62 (43 – 76) and 50 (30 – 72) years, respectively; however, country-specific medians suggest that the younger age of patients after Omicron variant emergence in the combined dataset is at least partially explained by an increase in the proportion of data contributed by South Africa, relative to the proportion of data contributed by other countries (Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the median age in the Omicron period.

claim: The younger age of patients after Omicron variant emergence in the combined dataset is at least partially explained by an increase in the proportion of data contributed by South Africa.
source: The median (IQR) ages of patients during the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods were 62 (43 – 76) and 50 (30 – 72) years, respectively; however, country-specific medians suggest that the younger age of patients after Omicron variant emergence in the combined dataset is at least partially explained by an increase in the proportion of data contributed by South Africa, relative to the proportion of data contributed by other countries (Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on country-specific data analysis.

claim: 48.3% of patients admitted during the pre-Omicron period were female.
source: A total of 48.3% and 54.8% of patients admitted during these periods, respectively, were female.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of female patients in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: 54.8% of patients admitted during the Omicron period were female.
source: A total of 48.3% and 54.8% of patients admitted during these periods, respectively, were female.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the proportion of female patients in the Omicron period.

claim: 5.2% of patients in the pre-Omicron period had the date of disease onset after admission date.
source: 5.2% and 9.1% of patients in the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods, respectively, had the date of disease onset after admission date.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of disease onset relative to admission.

claim: 9.1% of patients in the Omicron period had the date of disease onset after admission date.
source: 5.2% and 9.1% of patients in the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods, respectively, had the date of disease onset after admission date.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of disease onset relative to admission.

claim: 70.1% of patients during the pre-Omicron period were admitted to hospital due to COVID-19.
source: In some countries, information on whether COVID-19 was the main reason for hospitalisation was also collected: 70.1% (N=2248) and 69.0% (N=27,804) of patients during the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods respectively were admitted to hospital due to COVID-19; patients for whom this information was available were primarily from South Africa (94.9%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the reason for hospitalisation in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: 69.0% of patients during the Omicron period were admitted to hospital due to COVID-19.
source: In some countries, information on whether COVID-19 was the main reason for hospitalisation was also collected: 70.1% (N=2248) and 69.0% (N=27,804) of patients during the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods respectively were admitted to hospital due to COVID-19; patients for whom this information was available were primarily from South Africa (94.9%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the reason for hospitalisation in the Omicron period.

claim: Patients for whom information on whether COVID-19 was the main reason for hospitalisation was available were primarily from South Africa (94.9%).
source: In some countries, information on whether COVID-19 was the main reason for hospitalisation was also collected: 70.1% (N=2248) and 69.0% (N=27,804) of patients during the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods respectively were admitted to hospital due to COVID-19; patients for whom this information was available were primarily from South Africa (94.9%).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the source of data on reason for hospitalisation.

claim: 465/36,761 (1.3%) individuals reported a history of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection before the acute episode leading to hospitalisation.
source: Of note, 465/36,761 (1.3%) individuals reported a history of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection before the acute episode leading to hospitalisation included in this analysis (128/15,563 [0.8%] and 337/21,198 [1.6%] in the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the frequency of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection.

claim: 128/15,563 (0.8%) individuals in the pre-Omicron period reported a history of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Of note, 465/36,761 (1.3%) individuals reported a history of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection before the acute episode leading to hospitalisation included in this analysis (128/15,563 [0.8%] and 337/21,198 [1.6%] in the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the frequency of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: 337/21,198 (1.6%) individuals in the Omicron period reported a history of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Of note, 465/36,761 (1.3%) individuals reported a history of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection before the acute episode leading to hospitalisation included in this analysis (128/15,563 [0.8%] and 337/21,198 [1.6%] in the pre-Omicron and Omicron periods, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the frequency of previous SARS-CoV-2 infection in the Omicron period.

claim: There was a decrease in the percentage of patients with at least one comorbidity before versus during Omicron variant dominance (78.9% vs 59.6%).
source: When analysing the combined dataset, there was a decrease in the percentage of patients with at least one of the comorbidities listed in Appendix 1—table 3 before versus during Omicron variant dominance (78.9% [N=15,574] and 59.6% [N=60,625], respectively); however, country-specific data show variable patterns (Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the change in comorbidity frequency.

claim: Country-specific data show variable patterns in comorbidity frequencies.
source: When analysing the combined dataset, there was a decrease in the percentage of patients with at least one of the comorbidities listed in Appendix 1—table 3 before versus during Omicron variant dominance (78.9% [N=15,574] and 59.6% [N=60,625], respectively); however, country-specific data show variable patterns (Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement about variability in country-specific patterns.

claim: For many symptoms, frequencies were lower during the Omicron period versus the pre-Omicron period.
source: Whilst the directions of changes (increase or decrease) in frequencies of comorbidities were not consistent across countries, for many symptoms frequencies were lower during the Omicron period versus the pre-Omicron period.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the pattern of symptom frequencies.

claim: 96.6% of patients during the pre-Omicron period had at least one symptom.
source: The percentage of patients during the pre-Omicron period with at least one of the symptoms in Appendix 1—table 2 was 96.6% (N=11,683); this percentage was 88.6% (N=17,859) during the Omicron period (see Appendix 1—table 9 for country-specific numbers).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the frequency of symptoms in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: 88.6% of patients during the Omicron period had at least one symptom.
source: The percentage of patients during the pre-Omicron period with at least one of the symptoms in Appendix 1—table 2 was 96.6% (N=11,683); this percentage was 88.6% (N=17,859) during the Omicron period (see Appendix 1—table 9 for country-specific numbers).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the frequency of symptoms in the Omicron period.

claim: Data on vaccination status were available for 42,850/103,051 hospitalised patients.
source: Data on vaccination status were available for 42,850/103,051 hospitalised patients (8,952 during the pre-Omicron period and 33,898 during the Omicron period).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of vaccination data.

claim: 8,952 patients during the pre-Omicron period had vaccination status data available.
source: Data on vaccination status were available for 42,850/103,051 hospitalised patients (8,952 during the pre-Omicron period and 33,898 during the Omicron period).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of vaccination data in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: 33,898 patients during the Omicron period had vaccination status data available.
source: Data on vaccination status were available for 42,850/103,051 hospitalised patients (8,952 during the pre-Omicron period and 33,898 during the Omicron period).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of vaccination data in the Omicron period.

claim: There is considerable inter-country variation in the frequency of vaccination.
source: As expected, there is considerable inter-country variation in the frequency of vaccination.
evidence: This is a direct statement about variability in vaccination frequencies across countries.

claim: 55.8% of vaccinated patients received two or more doses before hospital admission.
source: Note that 55.8% of vaccinated patients received two or more doses before hospital admission.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of vaccine doses received.

claim: In many countries contributing data to this study there was an increase in vaccination coverage over time, including in the periods during and after the emergence of the Omicron variant.
source: However, as shown in Appendix 1—figure 4, with population-level vaccination coverage from before Omicron variant emergence up to the end of February 2022, in many countries contributing data to this study there was an increase in vaccination coverage over time, including in the periods during and after the emergence of the Omicron variant.
evidence: This is a direct statement about temporal trends in vaccination coverage.

claim: Overall, 11,314 patients admitted during the two study periods died during hospitalisation.
source: Overall, 11,314 patients admitted during the two study periods died during hospitalisation: 8517/94,524 by day 14 after hospital admission or disease onset, whichever occurred latest, and 10,530/94,461 by day 28; 738 patients died after day 28 and 46 patients who died did not have an outcome date recorded.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of deaths during hospitalisation.

claim: 8517/94,524 patients died by day 14 after hospital admission or disease onset.
source: Overall, 11,314 patients admitted during the two study periods died during hospitalisation: 8517/94,524 by day 14 after hospital admission or disease onset, whichever occurred latest, and 10,530/94,461 by day 28; 738 patients died after day 28 and 46 patients who died did not have an outcome date recorded.
evidence: This is a direct statement about 14-day mortality.

claim: 10,530/94,461 patients died by day 28 after hospital admission or disease onset.
source: Overall, 11,314 patients admitted during the two study periods died during hospitalisation: 8517/94,524 by day 14 after hospital admission or disease onset, whichever occurred latest, and 10,530/94,461 by day 28; 738 patients died after day 28 and 46 patients who died did not have an outcome date recorded.
evidence: This is a direct statement about 28-day mortality.

claim: 738 patients died after day 28.
source: Overall, 11,314 patients admitted during the two study periods died during hospitalisation: 8517/94,524 by day 14 after hospital admission or disease onset, whichever occurred latest, and 10,530/94,461 by day 28; 738 patients died after day 28 and 46 patients who died did not have an outcome date recorded.
evidence: This is a direct statement about deaths occurring after day 28.

claim: 46 patients who died did not have an outcome date recorded.
source: Overall, 11,314 patients admitted during the two study periods died during hospitalisation: 8517/94,524 by day 14 after hospital admission or disease onset, whichever occurred latest, and 10,530/94,461 by day 28; 738 patients died after day 28 and 46 patients who died did not have an outcome date recorded.
evidence: This is a direct statement about missing outcome dates.

claim: Median time to death was 10 days (IQR 5 – 17) for the pre-Omicron period.
source: Median (IQR) times to death were 10 (5 – 17) and 6 (3 – 13) days for the periods before and after Omicron emergence, respectively; similar information, on time from admission or symptoms onset to death, stratified by country is shown in Appendix 1—table 10.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the median time to death in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: Median time to death was 6 days (IQR 3 – 13) for the Omicron period.
source: Median (IQR) times to death were 10 (5 – 17) and 6 (3 – 13) days for the periods before and after Omicron emergence, respectively; similar information, on time from admission or symptoms onset to death, stratified by country is shown in Appendix 1—table 10.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the median time to death in the Omicron period.

claim: In some countries, during the Omicron period, a lower proportion of patients died during hospitalisation, compared to the period before Omicron emergence.
source: In some countries (see Figure 5 for comparisons on 14-day fatality risk, and Appendix 1—figure 5 for comparisons using the 28-day period), during the Omicron period, a lower proportion of patients died during hospitalisation, compared to the period before Omicron emergence; in India, the opposite pattern was observed although numbers for that country were limited.
evidence: This is a direct statement about country-specific mortality patterns, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: In India, the opposite pattern was observed with higher fatality risk during the Omicron period, although numbers for that country were limited.
source: In some countries (see Figure 5 for comparisons on 14-day fatality risk, and Appendix 1—figure 5 for comparisons using the 28-day period), during the Omicron period, a lower proportion of patients died during hospitalisation, compared to the period before Omicron emergence; in India, the opposite pattern was observed although numbers for that country were limited.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the pattern observed in India, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: In a mixed-effects logistic model on 14-day fatality risk that adjusted for sex, age categories, and vaccination status, hospitalisations during the Omicron period were associated with lower risk of death.
source: In a mixed-effects logistic model on 14-day fatality risk that adjusted for sex, age categories, and vaccination status, hospitalisations during the Omicron period were associated with lower risk of death (see Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of the statistical model, with reference to Table 2.

claim: The inclusion of common comorbidities in the model did not change the estimated association between study period and mortality.
source: The inclusion of common comorbidities in the model did not change the estimated association.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the robustness of the association to adjustment for comorbidities.

claim: Similar results were obtained when using 28-day fatality risk as the outcome.
source: Similar results were obtained when using 28-day fatality risk as the outcome.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the consistency of results with a different outcome definition.

claim: The estimated odds ratio for the association between study period and 14-day fatality risk was similar when excluding patients admitted for reasons other than COVID-19.
source: We repeated the 14-day fatality risk analysis excluding patients who reported being admitted to hospital due to a medical condition other than COVID-19; the estimated odds ratio for the association between study period and the outcome was similar to those reported in Table 2.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of a sensitivity analysis.

claim: In an additional sensitivity analysis, estimates from a model that only included data from countries with at least 50 records per study period were similar (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.61–0.69).
source: In an additional sensitivity analysis, estimates from a model that only included data from countries with at least 50 records per study period were also similar (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.61–0.69, adjusted for covariates included in model I, Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of another sensitivity analysis.

claim: Data on IMV were available in 74,563 records.
source: Data on IMV were available in 74,563 records.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of IMV data.

claim: Of 74,563 patients, 3111 required IMV during hospitalisation.
source: Of 74,563 patients, 3111 required IMV during hospitalisation; the date when IMV was initiated was reported for 1070/3111 patients.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of patients requiring IMV.

claim: The date when IMV was initiated was reported for 1070/3111 patients.
source: Of 74,563 patients, 3111 required IMV during hospitalisation; the date when IMV was initiated was reported for 1070/3111 patients.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of IMV initiation dates.

claim: Of those patients with data on IMV, 10,049/67,383 patients either died or required IMV.
source: Of those patients with data on IMV, 10,049/67,383 patients either died or required IMV.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the composite outcome of death or IMV.

claim: Data on variant were available for 1275 records.
source: To assess whether patterns described in previous subsections are generally consistent with analyses using individual-level variant information, we repeated comparisons for countries where information on the infecting variant was collected; data on variant were available for 1275 records.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the availability of individual-level variant data.

claim: Of 1275 records with variant data, 852 patients were admitted either during the pre-Omicron period or the Omicron period.
source: Of these, 852 patients were admitted either during the pre-Omicron period or the Omicron period: whilst only 1.9% (16/827) of those admitted during the Omicron period were infected by a variant other than Omicron, 4.0% (1/25) of patients during the pre-Omicron period had Omicron as the causative virus variant; for the calculation of these percentages data from a participating institution that prioritised contributing Omicron variant cases were not included.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of patients with variant data in the defined periods.

claim: Only 1.9% (16/827) of those admitted during the Omicron period were infected by a variant other than Omicron.
source: Of these, 852 patients were admitted either during the pre-Omicron period or the Omicron period: whilst only 1.9% (16/827) of those admitted during the Omicron period were infected by a variant other than Omicron, 4.0% (1/25) of patients during the pre-Omicron period had Omicron as the causative virus variant; for the calculation of these percentages data from a participating institution that prioritised contributing Omicron variant cases were not included.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the accuracy of variant classification in the Omicron period.

claim: 4.0% (1/25) of patients during the pre-Omicron period had Omicron as the causative virus variant.
source: Of these, 852 patients were admitted either during the pre-Omicron period or the Omicron period: whilst only 1.9% (16/827) of those admitted during the Omicron period were infected by a variant other than Omicron, 4.0% (1/25) of patients during the pre-Omicron period had Omicron as the causative virus variant; for the calculation of these percentages data from a participating institution that prioritised contributing Omicron variant cases were not included.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the accuracy of variant classification in the pre-Omicron period.

claim: Except for six clinical cases in South Africa and Saudi Arabia, all infections were caused either by Delta or Omicron variants.
source: Except for six clinical cases in South Africa and Saudi Arabia, all infections were caused either by Delta or Omicron variants, and for this reason only data on these two variants are presented (Appendix 1—table 12).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the distribution of variants in the individual-level data.

claim: For countries with ten or more observations of both Omicron and Delta variants, the patterns observed using individual-level variant data are broadly consistent with results obtained using the population-level approach.
source: The numbers of participants included in the latter comparisons are lower than the numbers included in the comparisons using population-level variant data; for countries with ten or more observations of both Omicron and Delta variants, the patterns observed are broadly consistent with results obtained using the population-level approach.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the consistency between individual-level and population-level approaches.

claim: Sensitivity analyses using different population-level threshold frequencies for the Omicron variant (10% and 80%, rather than 10% and 90%) are consistent with findings described in the Results section.
source: We also performed sensitivity analyses using different population-level threshold frequencies for the Omicron variant (10% and 80%, rather than 10% and 90%); these are shown in Appendix 1—figures 11–14 and are consistent with findings described in the Results section.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of sensitivity analyses.

claim: The finding that mortality was generally lower during the period when the Omicron variant was dominant is consistent with data from South Africa reported earlier this year.
source: Our finding that mortality was generally lower during the period when the Omicron variant was dominant is consistent with data from South Africa reported earlier this year (Wolter et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement compares the study findings with previously published data, supported by a citation.

claim: In a South African study with more than 30,000 patients with individual-level information on the infecting variant, individuals infected with the Omicron variant had a lower risk of disease progression that required hospital admission than individuals infected with other variants.
source: In that study, which included more than 30,000 patients with individual-level information on the infecting variant, individuals infected with the Omicron variant had a lower risk of disease progression that required hospital admission than individuals infected with other variants; amongst hospitalised patients, the odds ratio for the association between Omicron variant infection and severe disease was 0.7 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.3–1.4), which is similar to that observed in this study using death as the outcome.
